Changi South factory for sale at $12.8 mil
article:
A two-storey factory-cum-warehouse at 29 Changi South Street 1 has been launched for sale via an expression of interest (EOI) exercise. The property has an indicative price of $12.8 million and will be sold with vacant possession.

The site is held under a JTC lease with a balance tenure of around 30 years. Measuring 77,237 sq ft, the land is zoned for Business 2 use with a 1.0 plot ratio.

The plot has a regular shape, offering buyers “a practical configuration to redevelop the site into a brand-new facility” tailored to their needs, said Swee Shou Fern, head of investment advisory at ETC (a member of Realion Group), which is marketing the property.

The existing factory on the site has a floor area of around 49,693 sq ft. This translates to an equivalent plot ratio of approximately 0.64.

The factory’s location in the Changi South industrial precinct offers convenient access to Changi Airport, alongside exposure to Singapore’s logistics and manufacturing ecosystem, Swee notes.

“The ongoing development of Changi East, Changi Airport’s largest expansion project to date, is expected to further enhance the area’s role as an integrated logistics hub,” she added.

The EOI will close at 3pm on Nov 13.

title: The St Regis Singapore completes $44 mil transformation, enters new chapter
article:
The St Regis Singapore is entering a new chapter, following the completion of a $44 million, multi-year transformation, the hotel said in an Oct 6 release.

The 299-key luxury hotel on Tanglin Road, close to the Orchard Road shopping belt, underwent a major redesign that was carried out in phases from 2024.

It included renovations to all guestrooms, the John Jacob Ballroom (the hotel’s largest event venue), and event spaces on Level 1. It also introduced three new dining venues: The Tea Room, The St Regis Bar and Italian restaurant Sophia.

The final phase of the transformation — a revamp of the 355 sq m (3,606 sq ft) presidential suite — was completed last month.

Singapore-based firm FBEYE International led the hotel’s redesign. Its founder and creative director, Warren Foster-Brown, was part of the original team that worked on The St Regis Singapore when it first opened in 2008.

The reimagined hotel features a biophilic design that pays homage to the nearby Singapore Botanic Gardens.

Eco -conscious features were a significant component of the transformation. Rooms are now equipped with motion sensors for blinds and air-conditioning, water taps that dispense both hot and ambient drinking water, and eco-composite flooring comprising up to 50% recycled material.

“With our recent renovations, we took the opportunity to reimagine and showcase that sustainability is not a compromise, but an enhancement to the guest experience,” said Nick Heath, The St Regis Singapore’s general manager.

Other eco-conscious initiatives have been rolled out across the hotel. For example, dining menus feature sustainability-sourced seafood, cage-free eggs and plant-based menu options, while meeting venues include locally bottled water and linen-less banquet tables.

The hotel also enhanced its event spaces, as part of its goal to be a premier destination for Mice (meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions) events and weddings.

Two new LED walls were installed at the John Jacob Ballroom, along with a new built-in bar at the foyer. Meeting rooms on level one were also refreshed, including upgrades to audio-visual capabilities.

Pursuant to its transformation, The St Regis Singapore has garnered several accolades, including the 5-Star Best Hotel Interior (Singapore) award at the Asia Pacific Hotel Awards 2026-2027.

It was also awarded 4 Stars in Forbes Travel Guide 2026, ranked third for Best Hotels in Singapore at Travel + Leisure’s World’s Best Awards 2026, and was recognised among Tatler’s Best Hotels in Singapore 2026.

In addition, the hotel was named a recipient of the Condé Nast Traveller Triple Crown Award earlier this year. The accolade honours hotels that have won all three of the publication’s major awards: the Hot List (which recognises the best new hotel openings in their first year), the Gold List (hotels selected as an editor’s favourite), and Reader’s Choice (hotels awarded based on audience votes).

The St Regis Singapore is part of Hong Leong Group’s hospitality portfolio.

Kwek Leng Beng, the group’s executive chairman, highlighted the hotel’s significance to him and his wife, Cecilia Kwek, along with her role in its successful redesign. “Cecilia was actively involved in key conversations around the redesign, including the artwork, furnishings, lighting, colour palettes and interior details.”

He added: “Seeing The St. Regis Singapore receive international recognition following this transformation makes these milestones especially meaningful.”

title: 3 US Stocks That Doubled in a Year: Should You Buy, Hold or Take Profits?
article:
Doubling your money in 12 months is an extraordinary return.
What should you do next?’
Selling locks in the gains, but holding allows for further upside if the business continues to grow.
Past performance alone cannot tell investors what comes next.
Investors should evaluate whether the business has become significantly more valuable, whether earnings can continue growing strongly, and how much future growth may already be reflected in the current price.
We take a closer look at three US-listed stocks that have doubled, at a minimum, over the past year.

AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) – The AI Growth Winner
AMD’s stock price has increased by 3.8 times higher than a year ago (as of 25 September 2026), driven by
AI-led demand
for high-performance chips.
Its revenue in the first half of 2026 (1H2026) increased by 44% year on year (YoY) to US$21.8 billion, while net income was 2.3x higher at US$3.7 billion over the same period.
The company is highly cash generative, with cash flow from operating activities in 1H2026 up by 80% to US$5.3 billion compared to a year ago.
Expected demand for AMD’s chips has evolved with the developing AI narrative.
Initially, AI-related demand was focused on training large language models, which required lots of GPUs, an area where NVIDIA is the unquestioned leader.
However, agentic AI is becoming a more important part of the AI story, which has led to greater demand for CPUs that have traditionally been AMD’s strong suit.
In fact, the shift to agentic AI could lead to a 10x increase in demand for CPUs.
If demand for agentic AI continues to rise, this should translate into higher earnings and cash flow for AMD, which would justify holding on to the stock.
The company has introduced new products, including GPUs, CPUs and networking solutions for data centres, and has struck partnerships with Anthropic and Microsoft.
Of course, the bursting of an AI bubble is a key risk.
The company is also competing with NVIDIA, which is not resting on its laurels.
Recently, NVIDIA took the fight directly to AMD by launching the
Vera CPU
.
AMD has become more expensive over the past year, with its forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio rising from 27.3 in September 2025 to 39.5.

Moderna (NASDAQ: MRNA) – The Business Transformation Story
Moderna was one of the winners of the COVID-19 pandemic, with its mRNA vaccines playing a key role in controlling the virus.
However, its shares later tumbled as demand for the vaccines fell and a follow-up blockbuster product failed to emerge.
From its peak in September 2021, the company’s stock price had fallen nearly 95% by November 2025.
However, this past August, Moderna announced that its personalised cancer vaccine for melanoma, which it had been developing in partnership with Merck, showed initial positive results in a late-stage trial.
This was enough to send the company’s stock up by 177% in one day.
Given the relatively early stage of this breakthrough, Moderna’s financials do not yet reflect this potential.
The company expects 2026 revenue to be just 10% higher than 2025, while its bottom line is in the red.
The jump in its share price, without a corresponding increase in revenue, has resulted in the company’s valuation going through the roof – from a price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 3.3 in September 2025 to 32.4 currently.
The bull case here is that Moderna is able to successfully commercialise this vaccine, while also extending it to other forms of cancer.
If it succeeds, the TAM for its products would be significant.
However, drug trials are notoriously hard to predict, and initial success may not translate into a successful commercial outcome, which is still likely many years away.
The company also faces competition from other players such as BioNTech.

CrowdStrike (NASDAQ: CRWD) – The Secular Growth Compounder
CrowdStrike is riding a long-term trend of increasing demand for cyber-security protection, which has been accelerated recently due to the need to protect company data from bad actors armed with AI.
This has sent CrowdStrike’s stock price up by 106% over the past year to 25 September 2026.
In 2021, the company had US$874 million in revenue and a net loss of US$93 million.
By 2025, the top line had expanded to US$4 billion, a CAGR of 45.8%, although the company still suffered a net loss of US$17 million.
Meanwhile, its cash from operating activities was US$1.4 billion in 2025.
Management expects the company’s TAM to reach US$325 billion by 2030, driven by demand for AI-powered agentic cybersecurity.
CrowdStrike’s competitive advantage lies in the trillions of cybersecurity events per week that are consolidated on its Falcon platform.
This data makes the platform smarter over time, benefiting customers and creating a network effect.
Such growth does not come cheap.
At the end of April this year, its P/S ratio was 23.2, and has since expanded to 49.8.
There are two key catalysts for future growth.
The company is expected to continue growing its international business, which accounted for just 32% of total revenue in its fiscal year 2025.
Another source of growth is higher customer adoption.
CrowdStrike aims to move from offering customers a single product to multiple integrated cloud modules.
The bear case for CrowdStrike includes slowing growth as it becomes a larger company, and its products failing to guard against a future cyberattack, damaging its reputation.

Get Smart: A 100% Gain Is Not the Finish Line
A 100% gain is not a sign to sell a stock.
Indeed,
selling
simply because a stock has doubled is a sure-fire way to miss out on the benefits of long-term compounding.
For existing shareholders, the key question is whether the original investment thesis remains intact.
For new investors, the focus should be on future returns from today’s price rather than the gains someone else has already made.
A stock that has doubled can still have room to grow, while a stock that looks unstoppable can also disappoint.
The fundamentals and valuation ultimately matter more than the headline return.

title: US yields fall from 2002 high as oil dips, Bessent vows on debt
article:
(Oct 6): US bond yields fell from their highest levels since 2002 as oil prices retreated below US$100 a barrel and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent insisted the government’s debt load can be tamed.

It marked a pause in the global bond rout that’s been driven by inflationary fears from the US-Iran war as well as bets on more aggressive tightening from the Federal Reserve as US economic data comes in strong.

Bessent tried to reassure investors that a mix of economic growth and spending restraints will “very quickly” start to alter the path of US government borrowing. Speaking at a fireside chat in Pennsylvania on Monday night, he said the government would start “bending that curve".

Treasury 10 and 30-year yields fell by three and four basis points to 5.27% and 5.63%, respectively while those on the two-year were little changed. Crude prices retreated on Tuesday on signs more supplies were getting through the Strait of Hormuz.

Still, investors greeted Bessent’s comments with caution and were reluctant to call an end to the selloff.

See also: Trump aide Hassett says Powell should ‘move on’ from Fed board

“The market is likely to be very skeptical, given the deficit is 6% and there is no plan to reduce it,” said Gareth Berry, a strategist at Macquarie. “A stated ambition is not a plan.”

James Ringer, a fund manager at Schroders, said he is looking beyond the headline crude oil price.

“To see a meaningful rally across the curve, the number one thing you need to see is energy prices starting to decline,” he said. “That’s not just crude; that’s got to be the refined products as well.”

See also: Trump says new Fed chair Warsh should have voted against rate hike

Separately, Bridgewater Associates founder Ray Dalio warned that the US is approaching the limits of its debt cycle and potentially faces a crisis within three years if spending continues to outpace revenue.

Treasuries are vulnerable to a pullback of demand from China and Japan, two of the US’s largest foreign creditors, he said.

While HSBC Holdings plc strategists called bets for around 80 basis points of Fed hikes in 2027 "excessive", they’re sticking with a wager on the gap between five- and 30-year Treasury yields moving wider.

“The surge in volatility, coupled with a lack of any clear technical resistance at these levels from recent history has, in our view, kept many investors on the sidelines despite the growing optical appeal of elevated long-end rates,” Dhiraj Narula, US rates strategist at HSBC, wrote in a note.

title: Nvidia heads for US$6 tril value with chipmaker back at record
article:
(Oct 6): Nvidia Corp is on the verge of becoming the first company with a US$6 trillion ($7.66 trillion) market capitalisation as investors rotate back into the artificial-intelligence chipmaker.

The stock is once more at a record high after the company gave a robust revenue outlook and announced the biggest buyback in history, which takes advantage of a valuation that’s near multi-year lows. Those twin pillars — strong growth and a cheap multiple — stand out, especially as investors grapple with high interest rates and tepid economic data.

“Nvidia is attractive on both a growth basis and a value basis and it looks like a haven from any damage higher rates could do to the economy,” said Jim Awad, senior managing director at Clearstead Advisors, which owns Nvidia shares. “All of which makes it such an attractive proposition here and a place people should continue to gravitate to if they have concerns.”

The shares are up 28% this year in a rally that has added US$1.2 trillion to Nvidia’s market capitalisation, bringing it to just shy of US$5.8 trillion. The company also is by far the biggest contributor to the S&P 500 Index’s 14% gain in 2026.

The move is particularly striking considering the stock was down 11% for the year on March 30 as investors questioned the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure. Since then, sentiment around the AI landscape has flipped, with more existential questions about the potential threats it poses to humanity now leading the conversation. Meanwhile, inflation risks and the likelihood of interest-rate hikes by the Federal Reserve have made megacap technology companies like Nvidia look relatively safe to investors.

See also: What it takes for Malaysia to gain a foothold in advanced packaging

“As rate hike fears have materialised, money starts to move into these megacap tech stocks because they’re a little bit more resistant to rate hikes,” said Larry Tentarelli of Blue Chip Daily, adding that the semiconductor sector has also seen a rebound spurred by Meta Platforms Inc’s Muse AI agent. There’s “big rotation back into semis, a big rotation back into the megacaps and both of those play out well for Nvidia”.

The lure for investors was underlined by Nvidia’s authorisation of an additional US$150 billion under its existing share-repurchase programme, which CEO Jensen Huang said “reflects our confidence in the long-term opportunity ahead.” Prior to that, he called Nvidia “the world’s first and only growth value stock".

Wall Street tends to like buybacks as they represent payouts to stockholders and reduce a company's outstanding shares, providing a lift to earnings per share. Nvidia’s repurchase is unique among Big Tech companies, which are primarily using their cash for AI spending, with the exception of Apple Inc.

See also: Broadcom-backed AST's newly completed Singapore plant takes aim at AI chip squeeze

The buyback “is what investors want to see" as it shows the company “sharing the wealth of their crazy high profit margins with investors", Mizuho Securities analyst Jordan Klein wrote in a Sept 28 note to clients.

While there is an argument that buybacks are just a way for companies to inflate their earnings per share without organic growth, that hardly applies to Nvidia. In its previous report, the chipmaker projected that sales would expand 70% in fiscal 2028, well above the 45% growth that had been expected.

“The reason it’s able to do this huge buyback is because it is growing so fast that it has more money than it knows what to do with,” Clearstead’s Awad said. “It remains on the cutting edge of an AI revolution that shows no signs of abating and the demand it is seeing seems insensitive to rising rates, which adds to confidence in the sustainability.”

Nvidia’s net income is expected to double in fiscal 2027, which ends in January, with revenue leaping 90%. A year ago, both figures rose 65%.

But even with all that, Nvidia is still lagging the overall semiconductor sector this year. The Philadelphia Stock Exchange Semiconductor Index has gained 86% in 2026, fuelled by companies like Micron Technology Inc, Marvell Technology Inc and Intel Corp, whose stock prices are up more than 200% even as they trade below their record highs hit earlier in the year.

Of course, at least part of Nvidia’s problem is simply the market’s physics — it is now the biggest stock in the world and it takes a lot to jolt shares that have been far and away the best performers in the S&P 500 for a decade. Can this growth just keep on going?

That question is at the heart of why the stock now trades at about 17 times earnings expected over the next 12 months, close to its lowest level in 10 years and a discount to the S&P 500 Index, which is priced at 19 times forward earnings.

“Nvidia is a cheap stock but the problem that Nvidia runs into [is that] it’s almost a victim of its own success,” Tentarelli said. “It just takes so much to move the needle.”

title: Mideast oil chiefs warn world needs to share Iran-War costs
article:
(Oct 6): The heads of two of the Middle East’s biggest oil producers warned that the rest of the world will need to share the burden of paying for the Iran war and the need for infrastructure spending that it’s creating.

The conflict has led to widespread damage to oil pipelines, refineries, gas plants and dozens of tankers, racking up a bill for new investment that’s already in the tens of billions of dollars.

Amin Nasser, the CEO of Saudi Aramco, and Sheikh Nawaf Al-Saba, his counterpart at Kuwait Petroleum Corp, told the Energy Intelligence Forum on Monday they were looking to expand export-route and overseas-storage capabilities. The KPC boss said if European nations want Kuwaiti-made fuels like diesel and jet fuel, they will have to invest in the infrastructure to store it.

“No country should face this alone,” Nasser said. “Oil and gas infrastructure is not a cost to be minimised or avoided. It is a collective necessity for producers and consumers alike.”

Sheikh Nawaf said the need to store fuels is particularly acute in Europe, where Kuwait had become a major supplier of refined oil products before the conflict. The continent has since been thrust into an energy crisis, with diesel in especially short supply.

See also: Trump’s vanity summit with Xi

Kuwait is now discussing investments with European partners to store more refined fuels closer to consumers, he said.

“We want to be in that position where we’re providing you the distillates and you also need to make those logistical investments ready so that we can store,” he said.

Nasser said even if the crisis were to end now, about two million barrels a day of additional demand could be needed for as long as two years just to replenish depleted stockpiles.

See also: Iran says won’t soften demands after Trump rejects Hormuz offer

Aramco is working on alternative crude export routes to diversify away from reliance on its traditional Persian Gulf and Red Sea shipment options to reach global buyers, Nasser said, without providing any details. The company is also studying plans that would double or triple the capacity of its overseas storage facilities, he said.

The importance of paying forward for more flexible arrangements has been underscored by the kingdom’s return on the East-West pipeline, which has served as a vital route to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, as shipments through the world’s most important energy chokepoint have been disrupted. The cost of building the conduit paid out in 14 days once the conflict began, Nasser said.

As war drags into an eighth month, causing historic disruption, he called on others to invest in making their supply chains more nimble.

“Of course, not every system should look like ours, but every system needs deeper worlds of resilience,” he said.

title: Ambani’s Jio said to seek about US$114 bil valuation in IPO
article:
(Oct 6): Jio Platforms Ltd is likely to seek a valuation of about 11 trillion rupees in its planned initial public offering, according to people familiar with the matter, falling short of earlier expectations for what may still be the country’s largest-ever listing.

The telecom and digital services arm of billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries Ltd has finished gauging demand for the offering and is likely to begin meetings with potential investors this week to discuss valuation and pricing, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private.

India’s largest wireless operator is looking to open its IPO the week of Oct 19 and list before Oct 30, the people said. Deliberations are ongoing and the final dates, valuation and other details could change, they said.

A representative for Jio didn’t immediately respond to a request for comments.

The valuation would also make Jio India’s third most valuable publicly traded company, behind parent Reliance, which has a market capitalisation of about US$169 billion. Bharti Airtel Ltd, Jio’s main telecommunications rival, is valued at about US$116 billion.

Jio filed its draft prospectus in June for an offering of as many as 270 million new shares, equivalent to about 2.93% of its post-issue equity capital, according to Bloomberg calculations. Valuation figures floated earlier were higher, including in the US$130 billion to US$170 billion range at one point.

See also: World Bank lifts India GDP view, says Asia’s buffers too thin

But a stock rout has dented the pricing ambition of several IPOs in the country, including the marquee offering of National Stock Exchange of India Ltd, which was forced to downsize its deal. In June, local brokerage Motilal Oswal Financial Services estimated Jio’s valuation at between US$115 billion and US$118 billion while Dolat Capital valued the company at around $110 billion.

At a US$114 billion valuation, the Jio shares being offered would be worth about US$3.4 billion, still surpassing the 278.7 billion rupees raised by Hyundai Motor Co’s Indian unit in 2024.

Jio’s offering adds to an already busy year for India’s IPO market. Listing proceeds surpassed US$9 billion in the July-September quarter, the most ever for the period, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That pushed fundraising so far this year to more than US$13 billion.

See also: US, India officials signal trade deal talks at an impasse

The company has appointed 19 banks to work on the share sale, including Kotak Mahindra Capital Co, Morgan Stanley, BofA Securities Inc, Axis Capital Ltd, BNP Paribas and Citigroup Inc.

title: How to Evaluate a Public Company Before Investing
article:
This article is for educational purposes only and does not constitute financial advice or a recommendation to buy or sell any security. Investors should consider their objectives, financial situation, and risk tolerance before investing.
Buying a stock can be as quick as clicking a button. Understanding the business behind it takes a little more work.
A low P/E ratio, rapid revenue growth, or exposure to a hot sector may draw attention, but none of these factors on its own tells you whether the business is actually healthy.
Before deciding whether a stock looks cheap, it helps to understand the fundamentals: how the business makes money, whether profits are turning into cash, how much debt it carries, and whether management has used shareholders’ money well.
These checks will not tell you where the share price goes next. They can, however, help you avoid buying a weak business just because the headline numbers look attractive.
Understand How the Business Actually Makes Money
Start with the business itself.
What does the company sell? Who are its customers? Where does most of its revenue come from? Is demand recurring, cyclical or dependent on a handful of major contracts?
A company’s
annual report
is usually one of the best places to start. It lays out the business, financial results, operating segments, and many of the risks investors should know about.
You do not need to understand every technical detail. You should, however, be able to explain in plain English how the company makes money and what might disrupt that model.
If you still cannot explain the business after going through its filings, it may be worth doing more homework before moving on.
Check Whether Growth Is High Quality
Revenue can grow for good reasons and bad ones.
A retailer opening 50 new stores will probably report higher sales. So might a company that cuts prices heavily or gives customers longer to pay. The headline number may look the same, but the quality of that growth is very different.
That is why one quarter rarely tells you much on its own.
Look at several years of results and ask:
Is revenue growing consistently?
Are margins improving or shrinking?
Is profit keeping pace with sales?
Is growth coming from the core business or acquisitions?
One strong quarter can flatter a weak trend. What matters is whether growth is becoming more profitable and more sustainable over time.
Follow the Cash, Not Just the Profit
Profit can look healthy while cash tells a different story.
The
cash flow statement
tracks the cash moving in and out of the business. A good place to start is operating cash flow, or the cash generated by the company’s day-to-day operations.
If profits have risen for several years but operating cash flow remains weak, dig deeper. Customers may be taking longer to pay, inventory could be piling up, or the business may simply need more working capital as it expands.
None of these is automatically a red flag. What matters is understanding why profit and cash are moving in different directions.
Free cash flow adds another layer. It is commonly calculated as operating cash flow minus capital expenditures, showing how much cash remains after the company invests in assets needed to maintain and grow the business.
Make Sure the Balance Sheet Can Take a Hit
Good companies still go through bad years.
The
balance sheet
gives you a snapshot of what a company owns and owes. For investors, the more useful question is how much room the business has if sales slow, costs rise, or borrowing becomes more expensive.
Look at:
Cash versus debt
Interest expenses
When major debts are due
Whether borrowing is rising faster than earnings
How often the company raises new capital
Debt itself is not necessarily a problem. A stable utility and a young technology company, for example, may reasonably carry very different balance sheets.
The real question is whether the business can comfortably meet its obligations without sacrificing growth or repeatedly asking shareholders for more money.
Look at How Management Treats Shareholders
Financial statements show the outcome. Management choices usually tell you how the company got there.
Look at how the company has used shareholders’ money over time. Have acquisitions created value? Has management repeatedly issued new shares? Are related-party transactions clearly disclosed?
One simple test is to go back to older annual reports. Management teams regularly lay out expansion plans, targets, and priorities. Comparing those promises with what eventually happened can tell you a lot about execution and credibility.
Insider ownership is useful context too, but it should not be read in isolation. A founder owning a large stake may help align interests, while concentrated ownership can make the treatment of minority shareholders even more important.
Decide Whether the Price Still Makes Sense
Only after understanding the business and its finances does valuation become more useful.
The
price-to-earnings ratio
, or P/E ratio, is one common starting point. It compares a company’s share price with its earnings and can help investors compare valuations across similar companies or against the stock’s own history.
For companies earning little or no profit, however, P/E can be misleading or unusable, so investors need to look beyond that ratio.
A low P/E does not automatically mean a bargain.
The market may be expecting profits to fall, debt to become harder to manage or an industry to face long-term decline. Equally, a higher valuation may be reasonable for a company growing quickly with strong cash generation and a durable competitive position.
The useful question is not simply, “Is this stock cheap?”
It is: Does the price make sense for the quality, growth, and risks of the business?
A Practical Checklist Before You Invest
Before buying shares in a public company, ask yourself:
Do I understand how the company makes money?
Is growth coming from the core business?
Are profits turning into cash?
Can the balance sheet handle a weaker year?
Has management delivered on previous plans?
Are shareholders being diluted regularly?
What could realistically go wrong?
Does the valuation already assume everything goes right?
You do not need a complicated financial model to answer every one of these questions.
The goal is simply to know what you are buying, where the weaknesses are and whether the price makes sense before you put money into it.
